title: Book 7 opens: love God and neighbor; love of brothers
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK SEVEN. Concerning the love toward the brothers.

Cyril: With praises for us, O Palladius, crowning unto a limit and unto the highest the first and uppermost of the commandments—the law, I mean—the ‘You will love the Lord your God from whole heart and from whole understanding and from whole strength’; and adding also that ‘And your neighbor as yourself,’ and indeed also Christ himself saying clearly that on these two commandments all the law and the prophets hang, and naming love a fulfillment of law—Paul the divine also, because of doing nothing evil to the neighbor—the word has made for us, as at least it seems to me, a sufficient arrangement upon the first, according at least to what is possible, going up and down and somehow as in a circle, and not ignobly narrating what manner from our side the love unto God whole and altogether blameless would become. Come then already, let us busy ourselves with the neighboring and sister commandment, and let us make exact examination of the love unto the neighbor, tracking very well the things through which someone would become in a beautiful circle of virtue, and having taken the best glory of craftsmanship unto this, will walk in goodness with God and humans according to the divine Samuel. For I myself say that it is necessary to practice gracefully together with the love unto God also the love unto brothers; since to fall short of one has the missing upon both, according at least to John’s voices. For he has written thus: ‘If someone should say that I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar; for the

title: 1 John brother-love; tassels and blue thread as memory of law
english: one not loving his brother whom he has seen, how is he able to love the God whom he has not seen? And this commandment we have from him, that the one loving God love also his brother.’ Therefore both are destroyed together with one another and rise together brightly; for the virtues are as it were near-doored to one another, and like some unbroken pair they ferry the one having practiced best to drive unto one outshining and most complete beauty of piety unto God.

Palladius: You have spoken well. And since the aim is to sweat in these things, come again, and gathering the trusts upon each of the contemplations from the sacred Letters, try to tell me how the pure fulfillment of the love unto the neighbor would become.

Cyril: A most plentiful path then carries us off unto this. For it has been written that ‘Your commandment is very broad.’ Yet the craftsmanship upon each of the things done, I think one would not collect from elsewhere except through the law; for a prophetic word said that it has been given to us unto help. And at any rate raising us unto the continual remembrance of the things having been legislated, the lawgiver says: ‘And you will cast these words into your heart and into your soul, and you will fasten them as a sign upon your hand, and they will be unshaken before your eyes, and you will teach them to your children, to speak them sitting in a way and lying down and rising, and you will write them upon the doorposts of your houses and of your gates, in order that you may be many-dayed, and days of your sons upon the earth which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, just as the days of the heaven upon the earth.’ And what again is the ‘Fasten them upon your hands,’ he made clear in Numbers. For it has been written thus: ‘And the Lord said toward Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and you will say toward them, and let them make for themselves fringes upon the wings of their own garments unto their generations; and you will set upon the fringes of the wings a hyacinth-colored cord, and it will be in the fringes, and you will look at them, and you will remember all the Lord’s commandments, and you will do them; and you will not be turned aside behind your understandings, and behind your eyes in which you fornicate behind them, in order that you may remember; and you will do all my commandments, and you will be holy to your God; I am the Lord your God.’ Having commanded beforehand then very well that we write the law down in hearts, then knowing forgetfulness a hard sickness of mind, he commands that the commandments must be marked off as on a tablet upon the doorposts; and indeed also to fasten to the right hand little tablets somehow perhaps pregnant with the law and having the oracle written in, and indeed also that they be hung from the garments themselves, he says is not unprofitable unto benefit—through both fringes and the hyacinth-colored cord.

title: Blue thread = heavenly mind; law in heart; Leviticus blessings begin
english: Palladius: And what remembrance of the divine laws would become for us through fringes and a hyacinth-colored cord?
Cyril: For do you not say that the law has been spoken enigmatically to those of old and indeed also is as in shadows?
Palladius: I say so.

Cyril: An enigma then of needing to choose to think and do the things from heaven, and to remember thoroughly the laws from above—the fastening both of fringes and of the hyacinth-colored cord itself to the hand? For I think that somehow the ethereal body is imaged by the Indian stone—I mean the hyacinth—mixed with gleam and darkness, and somehow having in depth the water-like, and showing a trembling and easily-diffused look. Therefore the law has commanded economically that both from the garments themselves and indeed also from the hand the hyacinth-colored cord be hung, somehow as it were sounding under: Let a garment of mind and understanding be for you—an oracle from heaven—and let the law be awarder of right works. For the hand is a symbol of work; and the things done by us according to law are somehow altogether also unreproveable, and do not have the left-handed thing in baseness. Therefore the Pharisees were magnifying their fringes, and were widening their phylacteries—that is, the little tablets hung from the right hand; yet they were being laughed at by Christ, making the matter a starting-point of glory-loving, and not unto remembrance of the law. It is possible then even to lawless according to law, if someone should not use the law rightly. And this, I think, is what Solomon said: ‘There is a just one being destroyed in his just thing.’ Therefore the divine commandment must be written down unto mind and heart, and making the benefit of the matter clear the divine David said concerning every just one: ‘The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped.’ For it is, I think, also very clear that for whomever the divine law is present unto mind, there will also altogether be present the having been well fixed, and the lying in the firm of virtue.
Palladius: It holds thus.

Cyril: Therefore the long and continual meditation of the law carries away unto the straight—and this would be what seems to God—sending out forgetfulness as it were some turbid thing and mist of a human’s understanding. And the lawgiver does not stop unto these things, but inventing also something better besides, he makes hope as it were some bait of the eagerness at least in needing to do—the hope upon all the most prayed-for things. For he said again: ‘If you walk in my ordinances, and keep my commandments, and do them, I will give the rain to you in its season, and the earth will give its births, and the woods of the plains will give back their fruit. And the threshing will overtake the vintage for you, and the vintage will overtake the sowing, and you will eat your bread unto fullness, and you will dwe

title: Leviticus/Deuteronomy blessings; spiritual rain; toward neighbor-love
english: ll safely upon your land, and the war will not pass through your land, and I will give peace in your land, and you will sleep, and there will not be the one frightening you, and I will destroy evil beasts from your land.’ Do you understand of how much care and mildness he counts worthy the fair and most work-loving one, and indeed the one worsted by reverence concerning the law? For both early and late rain, and fruitfulness one upon another, and indeed also fullness of bread, and unstinting use of foods, and besides these he announces he will gift peace. For it is likely that the genuine guard of the law, and an unsated lover of whatever God should wish, be soaked with the unstinting gifts of the heavenly good things; for the spiritual and from-above encouragement, watering like rain a soul of the just as it were a fat and well-bearing earth, gladdens it very much, so as to show an unfailing and as it were all-variegated fruit of piety unto God; and peace crowns, bringing in the remaining unto being well. At any rate Paul also writes: ‘And the peace of God, the one surpassing every mind, will guard your hearts and your thoughts.’ The one then having obtained such munificence from God will continue a warless and peaceable life, the enemy yielding, and every one having stood against falling and going away unto nothing, and a diabolic approach being idle, and every fear going easily out of the way. And this same law we will also find written in Deuteronomy. For he said here having altered a little: ‘And if by hearing you hear all his commandments as many as I command you today, to love the Lord your God, and to serve him from whole heart and from whole soul, and he will give you the rain of your land, according to early and late season, and you will bring in your grain and your wine and your oil, and you will give fodder in your fields for your cattle.’ Therefore then the craftsmanship and good-rhythm, at least unto needing to fulfill whatever God should wish, the meditation of the law will house in our souls. And the desire of the things having been promised shows the sweat upon virtues bearable.
Palladius: Truly; for I would agree, and very reasonably. Yet of the love unto the neighbor, in what manner someone would carry the law through—it is time to say, O friend.

Cyril: One must go then already upon this very thing. And indeed we say, following the sacred Letters, that the Master God of the wholes commanded Moses to assemble the people, and to bring them together very well cleansed and purified under the mountain called Sinai; for he ordered that they must wash the garments, and be seen better than the pleasure unto women, for three days, signifying through the things in sense and seen the intelligible things; for with bright garments as it were—the boasts from virtues—having been made splendid, and excelling with the brightness according to mind, and having been freed from all flesh-loving and earthly pollutions,

title: Sinai approach; Moses leads to God; fire smoke trumpet typology
english: it is somehow fitting to go unto a sight of God, the law pedagoguing us unto this, just as indeed Moses also the ones of old; for those things were types of the more true. And the pedagoguing through all-wise Moses, carrying the education through the law unto Christ, was under-typing for the more ancient ones. And besides these things I think it is also somehow worth watching that. For the matter and face of the one needing to pedagogue has been well kept in Moses’ face; for he did not present the people to himself, but to God, somehow as lawgiver and teacher and introducer of the things to be done. And the law also, being a pedagogue through the letter, was bringing us not to itself, but to the God Word having come down from heaven through us. Does the word seem to you to go for us according to the track of the thoughts of the truth?
Palladius: Altogether so.

Cyril: It has been written then that ‘And Moses led the people out unto a meeting of God, from the camp, and they stood under the mountain Sinai. And the mountain Sinai was being smoked wholly because of the Lord’s having come down upon it in fire, and the smoke was going up as smoke of a furnace; and all the people were astonished very much; and the voices of the trumpet were becoming going forward stronger very much. Moses was speaking; and God was answering him with a voice.’ The having come down of God upon a mountain would become a sign also very clear—that he loves to visit understandings not most low-lying, nor indeed to lodge with those having an earthy and ground-cast thought, but with whomever the mind should leap up toward the height, and having as it were a peak rising over, looks somehow below at the human things, and would imagine only the things beside God. And it would also signify otherwise that the knowledge concerning God is high and lying above the things according to us, and somehow perhaps catchable only in part by those having practiced to fly the high things; ‘For young of a vulture fly the high things,’ according as it has been written. And in this understand that God came down defining the ancient law for those of old, not where the people was, but high and far. For he was still standing off far according to the Psalmist’s voice, the Only-begotten not yet having come to be with us fleshly, nor indeed having let himself down unto emptying; for the mystery has been kept not for the more ancient ones, but unto us ourselves; for he has come to be with us as far as one may say, unto a glory clear to eyes, having left behind the heights of the Godhead; and he was living as a citizen with us, as one from us. And God was coming down in a form of fire; it was necessary for those about to be pedagogued by necessity and law to know clearly that they will have words toward fire, if they should choose to be careless. For the God-loving was not being practiced by the more ancient ones from willing love and a free lean of mind, but as from necessity and fear; for a spirit was in them not free, nor indeed of sonship, but of slavery unto fear. And the mountain is smoked because of the Lord’s having come down upon it in fire; and this, I think, is what is hymned in Psalms:
translator_notes: OET: no previous complete English of De adoratione Book 7 in PD; modern checks not copied as wording.

title: Smoke darkness tears; fire and clearer gospel voice; Sabbath opens
english: ‘And he set darkness his hiding.’ And the smoke would also signify otherwise for us the tear about to be altogether and entirely upon the despising; for the moisture from eyes creeps out with the strikes of the smoke. And if someone should wish to cast upon the present contemplations otherwise, he will count the fire unto the enlightenment through the law, yet not without mist; for the law is also dim and unclear, and the overshadowing from the letter thick, and able to muddy the eye of the understanding. And the voices of the trumpet going forward stronger; for small was and scarcely sounding the thing of the law in the beginnings. And since the word has gone forward for us unto Gospel education, Emmanuel having shone upon, the voices have become stronger; for Christ has sounded out something audible and clear, and already reaching unto all the inhabited world. For it is possible to hear him saying through David’s voice: ‘Hear these things, all the nations; give ear, all who dwell the inhabited world.’ Although the voice of the law at that time was not going elsewhere, nor indeed initiating all the nations, but sounding around only the Jews’ land, and pedagoguing one race—the one from Israel. But ‘Moses was speaking,’ it says; ‘and God was answering him with a voice.’ For Moses as a servant was seeking the law, and a mediator and under-worker of the divine oracles; yet God was answering with his own voice—that is, through Son; for voice and word of the Father is the Son. And from him is the law, even if it has been spoken through angels; at any rate it is possible, if somehow someone should choose, to hear him saying clearly: ‘I myself who speak am present.’ And, ‘I did not come to loosen the law or the prophets, but to fulfill; for I say to you, until the heaven and the earth pass, one iota or one tip will not pass from the law until all things become. The heaven and the earth will pass, yet my words will not pass.’ Therefore he calls the law his own words; for a voice of God has spoken it, just as I said just now—that is, the Son. Then it says that ‘The Lord has come down upon the mountain Sinai, upon the peak of the mountain, and the Lord called Moses upon the peak of the mountain, and Moses went up. And God said toward Moses saying: Having come down, testify to the people lest they ever draw near toward God to look closely, and a multitude fall from them; and let the priests drawing near to the Lord God be made holy, lest ever the Lord remove from them.’ The God above all comes down unto the mountain, then Moses having been called goes up. For it is not of the possible things that some be strong enough to leap up unto the heights of the true God-seeing, unless God having let himself down and preparing to become approachable to our understandings; and with him calling we go up thus scarcely unto a supernatural and as it were exceptional peak—the true knowledge concerning him which Christ will bring on, uncovering for us the Father and God, and the mountain untrodden for the herd-like (for impassable for the many is the

title: Moses with Aaron = law with Christ; Decalogue begins
english: grace of knowledge stretched very far over), yet walkable only for those knowing how to go through it, or rather also having been called unto this from God, just as indeed also Moses. If then somehow there is a faithful and genuine one in God’s house, he himself also will be according to that one chosen out and suitably holding unto coming to be near God, according at least to the manner in holiness and knowledge. For thus we will be with him saying: ‘And you, stand with me.’ And he enjoins that those crowned with priesthood must be thoroughly cleansed, saying: ‘Lest ever the Lord remove from them.’ For the matter of the priesthood is altogether slippery, and not far from dangers, or rather even very near, if the blameless unto life should not be seen present; for it is fitting that those serving the all-pure God be holy. Then he says: ‘And the Lord said to Moses: Go, come down and go up—you and Aaron with you; yet let the priests and the people not force themselves to go up toward God, lest ever the Lord destroy from them.’ Moses goes up and not without Aaron, who was unto a type of Christ. For law is honorable in Christ, and as holy through him, near God and with God. For he himself also proclaims the high priest and apostle of our confession, according to the Scriptures. Therefore let the law be yoked beside Christ, through the contemplation in spirit. For Moses has heard: ‘Go up—you and Aaron.’—‘What then God has yoked, let a human not separate,’ carrying the law away from the contemplation in Christ, because of clinging to the shadow alone, and not receiving the truth unto an image of the types. It has been said at least that the sacred race together with the peoples go up unto the mountain. For not to those being pedagogued in law, nor to those still completing the worship in shadows, has the dogma in high and uppermost things concerning him been given from God; yet it has rather been kept for those having been justified in faith, and having been called in Christ unto obedience, and a knowledge differing much from the more ancient. For Paul the divine has also admired the surpassing of the knowledge of Christ; and the Savior himself will also witness, concerning both us and those from Israel’s blood, saying openly that ‘To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens, yet to those it has not been given. And concerning the Jews: ‘Leave them; they are blind, guides of blind ones.’ And he has sounded again toward those having known him: ‘Yet of you blessed are the eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.’ And since the God of the wholes was completing the words about these things, he begins to legislate, and to mark off the laws upon all the best things. And thus he says: ‘I am the Lord your God, who led you out from Egypt’s land, from a house of slavery; there will not be for you other gods besides me.’ And he made a beginning fitting for the laws, saying himself to be the wonder-worker in Egypt; the one setting the whole creation, so to speak, against the manias of the greedy; rains and hailstones having ar

title: No other gods; vain Name; Sabbath command; what sanctifying means
english: med, and having shown changes of the elements, and having cast the pitiable death upon the firstborn, and having poured upon them the three-day darkness; the one gifting to go through middle of waves to whomever he should wish, and without toil shattering those having stood against. For it was necessary, necessary, that those running under the yoke of the divine commandment not be ignorant how great the lawgiver’s power is, and that it is not safe for them to strike against the one strong to set all things right easily.

Palladius: How well and God-fittingly the lawgiver was contemplating for us! For fear somehow always pours down unto well-persuasion, and works the harsh and hard-to-lead as it were some well-reined colt.

Cyril: You have spoken most rightly. Having refused then the needing to worship other gods, and the making of every idol, and likeness and writing, and the daring to distribute the name of the Godhead to the crafts of statue-makers, having brought under the last justices (‘For you will not take,’ he says, ‘the name of the Lord your God upon a vain thing, because the Lord will not cleanse the one taking his name upon a vain thing’), he rhythm-trains hereafter the human things, and marks off the law as it were some canon unto the straight for all citizens’ ways; and he stands us out of every sin, and before the others marking the season of the justice in Christ, according to which the most complete ransoming and the destruction of baseness, and re-forming unto what was from the beginning, and renewal of life in holiness and God-loving. Therefore he says: ‘Remember the day of the Sabbaths to make it holy; six days you will work, and you will do all your works, yet on the seventh day Sabbaths, a rest for the Lord your God; you will not do in it every work—you and your son and your daughter, your servant and your maidservant, your ox and your beast of burden, every animal of yours, and the sojourner dwelling beside you. For in six days the Lord made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all the things in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Because of this the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.’
Palladius: And what then is this? For I do not understand clearly. And in what manner would we make holy the day of the Sabbaths?
Cyril: Do you wish that we say some few things about Sabbath and the idleness honored in it? for thus the things having been oracle-spoken from God for us would also be very clear.
Palladius: Altogether so.

Cyril: The Sabbath, O Palladius, being a last day of the week, would somehow, I think, mark the season of our Savior’s sojourn, which has appeared upon a completion and all but already toward the very settings of the present age, yet has become for us a beginning and door and way unto a washing-off

title: Spiritual sabbatism in Christ; Hebrews rest; wood-gatherer type
english: of sin, unto freedom and forgiveness, unto incorruption and unto life, and unto the coming hope. And in many manners the faith of the sacred Letters also riddles for us the sabbatism understood in Christ, sometimes under-drawing the cessation in himself—the one as from sins—and defining the most bitter and harsh justice of the transgressor, and sometimes again typically showing the ransoming and forgiveness in him unto freedom, and indeed also the preparation unto the coming age.
Palladius: Say then how. For I would know as most sweetly.

Cyril: Through faith, O Palladius, understood spiritually in Christ we sabbatize, ceasing from the distractions in this world, and resting from empty carrying-around, and standing off from baseness, and stripping out of the yoke of the sin, we are let go hereafter unto free holiness. And at any rate the divine Paul says concerning those not yet having believed: ‘And with whom was he vexed forty years? Was it not with those having disobeyed, whose limbs fell in the desert? And to whom did he swear not to enter into his rest, if not to those having disobeyed? And we see that they were not able to enter because of disobedience. Let us fear then lest ever, a promise of entering into his rest being left, someone from you should seem to have come short.’ And after other things: ‘Therefore a sabbatism is left for the people of God.’ And yet how is it not true that if the sabbatism is only to be idle on Sabbath, how did Israel not enter into the rest, although having kept the idleness on Sabbath? But the matter was unto a type of the rest in Christ, and of the ceasing from sin of the one being justified by the faith. Therefore God commanded that the one collecting woods on Sabbath must have died stone-struck; and the justice upon that one was an under-type of an intelligible and necessary matter. Or is not the wood having already been withered from its own root, having been thoroughly cleaned and dried, a symbol of deadness? And would it also otherwise be nurture of fire?
Palladius: Truly.

Cyril: Some such thing is the all-toiling sin, as it were some deadness, and an unholy nurturer of the untamed flame for those loving it. Whenever then as in a season of cessation—I mean the one from sins—some should hold dead and fruitless works, and should choose to love, having let go virtue, the things through which penalties and flames would be kindled for them unto an age, they will reasonably undergo the condemnation upon death, because although it is possible not to live loosely, they willingly go through unto needing to be punished. Therefore we who have believed enter into the rest, according at least to the voice of blessed Paul. And at any rate through Jeremiah’s voice God accuses those signifying beside the beauty of the truth through sin unto the type, saying:
translator_notes: OET: no previous complete English of De adoratione Book 7 in PD; modern checks not copied as wording.

title: Jeremiah Sabbath burdens; Church as city; not cease from every good
english: ‘Go and stand in gates of sons of your people, in which kings of Judah enter, and in which they go out in them, and in all the gates of Jerusalem; and you will say toward them: Hear a word of the Lord, kings of Judah and all Judea and all Jerusalem, and those entering in these gates. Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not lift burdens on the day of the Sabbaths, and you will not do every work, and do not go out by the gates of Jerusalem, and do not carry out burdens from your houses on the day of the Sabbaths, just as I commanded your fathers and they did not hear, and they did not lean their ear, and they hardened their neck above their fathers, so as not to hear me, and so as not to receive education.’ Therefore he has commanded not only the needing to cease from every work on Sabbath, but also beyond gates of Jerusalem.
Palladius: Then what would the account of these things also be?

Cyril: Intelligible then and spiritual, and beyond the types, and better than the more ancient shadow. For he commands those sabbatizing in Christ to go unto a cessation of work having been turned toward baseness and looking, yet to make no burden at all upon the shoulder. For those once having cast off through the faith the truly hard-to-bear load of the sin—how is it not altogether struck-out to need to load themselves with it again unto a later time, and to choose to fall under again the yokes unto baseness? And to sit inside gates of Jerusalem types the needing for us not to stand off from the holy city, nor indeed to be carried outside and to slip away, through a turning-aside unto some other thing. And you will understand a holy city—the Church; for already somehow some, having been made bright through the faith into Christ, and having unloaded the profane sin, and having come to be inside holy gates of God’s house, have been carried unto standing-off, even if not toward an apparent one, yet they have leaped out of the holy gate, having honored idol-fitting customs. Therefore God has oracle-spoken that those sabbatizing intelligibly sit inside gates, the type signifying the safe and unexit-able, and the needing nowhere to slip from the genuineness unto him. And that the Church is God’s city, David especially will cry out saying: ‘Glorious things have been spoken concerning you, the city of God’; and the Savior himself will also somehow fill full concerning her saying: ‘Here I will dwell because I have chosen her.’
Palladius: It has been fixed then that we will dissolve every work on Sabbath, according at least to what seems to the lawgiver.

Cyril: Not every simply, O Palladius; for the needing to think and do the things upon which God would be pleased, and would have not a measured benefit, would not receive a praised cessation. For the sacred Letter has added not in vain, as at least it seems to me,
